title: Children’s online lives combine connection and learning with late-night platform exposure, harmful content, and purchase regret
source_unit: Ofcom, From apps to AI search: how the UK goes online in 2025 / Online Nation 2025
geography: United Kingdom children and adults, with detailed online-use, safety, well-being, and spending findings for children aged 8-17

observations.period: 2025; children’s daily online time and platform concentration

denominator.unit: UK children aged 8-14 in Ofcom online-use estimates

daily_time.value: children aged 8-14 spend almost three hours online daily; 13-14-year-olds spend about four hours

youtube_time.unit: minutes per day spent on YouTube by children aged 8-14

snapchat_time.unit: minutes per day spent on Snapchat by children aged 8-14

platform_reach.value: YouTube is used by 96 percent of children aged 8-14 and Google Search by 95 percent

observations.method: Ofcom Online Nation 2025 analysis of UK online-service use and time estimates across children’s devices and platforms.
observations.uncertainty: Time estimates depend on measurement systems, device coverage, account use, shared devices, and platform categorization; they do not establish quality, compulsion, or harm from time alone.
observations.subgroup: Children aged 8-14, younger Gen Z and Gen Alpha, and users of YouTube, Snapchat, WhatsApp, TikTok, and Google Search.
observations.counterinterpretation: The same time supports friendship, schoolwork, relaxation, learning, creativity, and access to information; concentrated use is not automatically harmful.

denominator.unit: UK children aged 8-14 using YouTube, Snapchat, TikTok, and WhatsApp

evening_to_morning_share.value: 15 to 24 percent of time on the four main services occurs between 9pm and 5am

after_11pm_share.value: 4 to 10 percent of usage occurs after 11pm depending on the platform

time_tradeoff.value: late-night platform use creates a potential tradeoff with sleep, school, family routines, and recovery time

observations.method: Ofcom platform-time analysis by time of day for children’s main online services.
observations.uncertainty: The data describe timing, not sleep duration, health outcomes, parental context, or whether late use is active, passive, educational, or socially necessary.
observations.subgroup: Children aged 8-14, families managing device rules, and children using different platform mixes during evening and overnight hours.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some late-night use may reflect asynchronous communication, time-zone differences, household schedules, or low-intensity background use.

denominator.unit: UK children aged 11-17 in Ofcom harmful-content and response measures

harmful_content_exposure.unit: percent saying they had seen or heard harmful content online in the prior four weeks

took_action.unit: percent taking some action after encountering harmful content

action_set.value: dislike, report, block, or tell an adult were among the reported responses

observations.method: Ofcom Online Nation 2025 survey and qualitative research on children’s harmful-content experiences and responses before Protection of Children Codes came into force.
observations.uncertainty: Self-reported exposure and action do not measure severity, repeat exposure, platform effectiveness, downstream harm, or whether responses produced a remedy.
observations.subgroup: Children aged 11-17, children encountering harmful content, families, platforms, schools, and safety regulators.
observations.counterinterpretation: High reported action may indicate emerging user agency and safety literacy, though it can also reflect a burden shifted from platforms onto children.

observations.period: 2025; online spending, influence, and consumer regret

denominator.unit: UK children aged 8-17 reporting recent online spending

recent_spending.unit: percent spending money online in the past month

purchase_prompts.value: character customization, adverts, friends or family recommendations, and influencer content were reported spending prompts

purchase_regret.value: 32 percent regretted in-game purchases and 43 percent regretted social-media purchases

unclear_purchase.unit: percent unclear what they were buying in games

observations.method: Ofcom Online Nation 2025 research on children’s online spending across social media, video-sharing, and gaming environments.
observations.uncertainty: Reported spending and regret do not establish monetary amounts, parental consent, contract enforceability, manipulation, or the causal role of influencers, advertising, or game design.
observations.subgroup: Children aged 8-17, young consumers, parents, gamers, social-media users, influencers, advertisers, and platform marketplaces.
observations.counterinterpretation: Online purchases can be voluntary, social, creative, or useful; regret and unclear product understanding indicate a need for age-appropriate choice and protection rather than proof that all digital spending is harmful.

related_sources.claim: Ofcom 2026 children’s online-safety research and protection-measure updates provide regulatory follow-up context.
UK government response provides complementary policy context on age assurance, overnight platform restrictions, and digital resilience.

boundary: This record adds a child-platform-time, safety-response, and digital-consumption route. It reports Ofcom publication aggregates and summaries; it is not child-level respondent analysis, device telemetry, a clinical sleep or mental-health study, or a causal estimate of platform design effects.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Ofcom Online Nation 2025 publication page was reviewed; children’s time, late-night use, harmful-content response, online spending, influence, regret, and uncertainty claims were cross-checked.
